rationale: This is a tiny C++ program (8 functions, 770 text bytes) dominated by constructors/destructors and a small main, so the strategy is to concentrate control-flow obfuscation on main while keeping transformation costs proportionate. FLA gets the highest weight because flattening the 339-byte main yields the largest reverse-engineering gain per function in the binary. SUB and SPLIT are favored as cheap, low-risk complements that add diversity across all 8 functions (including the small destructors) with negligible runtime/size penalty. BCF is moderately weighted: it is effective but inflates size/runtime, which matters when total text is only ~770 bytes, so it should only attach to functions whose features favor it rather than blanket-applied. IBR and ICALL are given mid-range security weights but higher CorrectnessRisk because this program is C++ with virtual dispatch and constructors — indirect-call/branch rewrites interact poorly with vtables, global constructors, and unwinding, so the compiler should apply them conservatively. IGV is omitted entirely: indirecting global variable accesses is both low-value here (few globals, tiny data) and the highest-risk pass for breaking C++ static initialization/vtable references.
